column1: What is SO(3) and how many independent degrees of freedom does a rotation matrix R in SO(3) actually have, despite containing 9 elements?
column2: SO(3) is the Special Orthogonal group in 3D — the set of 3x3 orthogonal matrices with determinant +1. Despite 9 elements, 6 constraint equations (3 orthonormality + 1 determinant, reducing to 6 independent) reduce it to only 3 independent degrees of freedom, matching a rigid body's rotational freedom.

column1: What are the two defining mathematical constraints on a rotation matrix R?
column2: 1) Orthonormality: columns are mutually perpendicular unit vectors (R^T R = I). 2) Determinant constraint: det(R) = +1, guaranteeing right-handed chirality (proper rotation, not a reflection).

column1: What is gimbal lock, and which rotation representation suffers from it?
column2: Gimbal lock is a singularity in Euler angle representations where two of the three rotation axes become aligned, causing loss of one rotational degree of freedom and mathematical degeneracy during composition/interpolation of rotations.

column1: Why are rotation matrices preferred over Euler angles and axis-angle representations for composing successive rotations?
column2: Rotation matrices compose via simple matrix multiplication and invert via transpose (R^-1 = R^T), leveraging robust linear algebra infrastructure—unlike Euler angles (gimbal lock) or axis-angle (computationally expensive, nonintuitive composition).

column1: How many independent parameters does the Denavit-Hartenberg (DH) convention use to specify the transform between two adjacent robot link frames, and why is this a reduction?
column2: DH uses exactly 4 parameters (link length, link twist, link offset, joint angle) per joint, reduced from the 12 degrees of freedom present in an arbitrary spatial transformation, by exploiting the geometric constraint that joint axes define shared frame structure.

column1: What problem did Denavit and Hartenberg solve in 1955, and why was it significant?
column2: They solved the standardization crisis in kinematic chain analysis by proposing a minimal, unambiguous 4-parameter convention for specifying relative pose between adjacent coordinate frames—enabling consistent, collaborative, and standardized controller synthesis across engineers.

column1: In forward kinematics, what is the fundamental input-output relationship, and is the solution always unique?
column2: Forward kinematics maps joint configuration (joint angles/displacements) to end-effector Cartesian pose: x = f(q). This mapping is deterministic and always produces exactly ONE unique result for any given joint input.

column1: For a 6-DOF serial manipulator, how many nonlinear equations must inverse kinematics solve, and how many are actually independent?
column2: 12 nonlinear equations total (3 position + 9 rotation matrix elements), but only 6 are independent because the rotation matrix's orthonormality constraints eliminate 3 redundant equations—matching the 6 unknown joint angles.

column1: How many distinct inverse kinematic solutions does a typical 6-axis industrial robot (e.g., KUKA KR 6, ABB IRB 120) exhibit for a given reachable end-effector pose, and what causes this multiplicity?
column2: Typically 8 distinct solutions, arising from 3 binary configuration choices: shoulder left/right, elbow up/down, and wrist flipped/not flipped.

column1: What key computational advantages do analytical (closed-form) inverse kinematics solutions have over iterative numerical methods?
column2: Analytical solutions execute in constant time regardless of initial configuration, produce ALL possible solutions simultaneously for explicit selection, and never suffer from convergence failures or local minima traps—unlike iterative numerical solvers.

column1: What is the manipulator Jacobian J(q), and what is the central velocity kinematics equation it defines?
column2: J(q) = ∂f/∂q is the partial derivative matrix mapping joint velocity to Cartesian velocity. The central equation is ẋ = J(q)q̇, linearly relating joint-space velocities to end-effector task-space velocities at a given configuration q.

column1: What happens physically and mathematically near a kinematic singularity of the Jacobian?
column2: Near a kinematic singularity, the Jacobian loses rank (becomes non-invertible or ill-conditioned), causing small desired Cartesian velocities to require infinite joint velocities—rendering the commanded motion physically impossible in that direction.
